flashcards.back: The set of rules that govern how words are combined to form correct sentences. Word → phrase → clause → sentence → paragraph.
Names a person, place, thing, animal, idea or quality.
Use subjective case as subject ("She and I attended"), objective case as object ("between you and me"); a pronoun must agree with its antecedent in number and person.
Expresses action, occurrence or state of being.
Base form, past simple, past participle (e.g. write–wrote–written).
Expresses sudden emotion (Oh! Wow! Alas! Hurray!).

Simple present — habits, facts, schedules ("The meeting starts at 10"); present continuous — now, temporary, planned future; present perfect — past action with present relevance (with already, yet, just, ever, never, since, for); simple past — finished action at a definite time;

"I am knowing" ✗ (stative verbs — know, believe, like, want, own — avoid continuous); "He go to office" ✗ → "He goes"; "I have seen him yesterday" ✗ → "I saw him yesterday"; "since two years" ✗ → "for two years"; sequence of tenses — "I thought he is honest" ✗ → "was honest".
A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb.
"He is one of the employees who are efficient."
Declarative (statement), interrogative (question), imperative (command/ request), exclamatory (emotion), plus optative (wish).
One independent clause ("The company launched a new product.").
Two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction or semicolon ("The company launched a product, and sales increased.").
One independent + one or more dependent clauses ("Because the demand was high, the company increased production.").
Two or more independent + at least one dependent clause.
Zero (If you heat ice, it melts), first (If it rains, we will cancel), second (If I were the CEO, I would...), third (If I had known, I would have attended).
First word of a sentence; proper nouns; days, months; titles; the pronoun "I"; headings.

Commonly confused words — affect/ effect, accept/ except, principal/ principle, stationary/ stationery, complement/ compliment, advice/ advise, there/ their/ they're, lose/ loose, than/ then, its/ it's, whose/ who's, council/ counsel, personal/ personnel, formally/ formerly, ensure/ insure/ assure.
A group of related sentences developing one main idea. Usually 5–10 sentences (about 100–200 words).

Topic sentence (states the main idea — usually the first sentence); supporting sentences (explanations, examples, facts, statistics, reasons); concluding (closing) sentence (summarises or links to the next idea).

Unity (all sentences relate to the main idea), coherence (logical flow; transitions; repeating key words; pronouns; parallel structure), completeness (adequate development), emphasis, clarity and conciseness, variety in sentence length.

Addition (also, moreover, in addition), contrast (however, but, although, on the other hand), cause/ effect (therefore, as a result, because), sequence (first, next, finally), example (for instance, for example), conclusion (in conclusion, to sum up).
Examples, facts and statistics, comparison/ contrast, cause and effect, definition, classification, process, description, narration, reasons.
(1) choose the topic; (2) identify the purpose and audience; (3) write the topic sentence; (4) brainstorm supporting points; (5) arrange logically; (6) write the draft; (7) revise and edit.

Paints a picture in words of a person, place, object or experience using sensory details (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch), vivid adjectives and figurative language; follows spatial order (top to bottom, left to right, near to far).
Tells a story or recounts events in chronological order with characters, setting, plot; uses past tense and time transitions (first, then, later, finally); has a point or lesson.
Explains, informs or defines — gives facts, process, cause–effect, comparison; objective tone; uses logical order and signal words.
Convinces the reader to accept an opinion or take action; clear claim (stance), reasons/ evidence, appeals (logic, emotion, credibility), addresses counter-argument, strong call to action.
A short, organised piece of non-fiction writing on a single topic, expressing the writer's ideas with a clear structure. Typical length 300–1,000 words.
Each with a topic sentence, evidence, explanation and link to the thesis.
A specific, debatable, one-sentence claim ("Remote work improves productivity and employee wellbeing, so firms should adopt hybrid models.") — not a fact or a question.
Reach and customer engagement. Body 2: low-cost marketing and brand building. Body 3: risks — misinformation, reputation damage, privacy.
Vague thesis, poor transitions, one-sided argument, repetition, long paragraphs, grammatical errors.
Essay — personal argument; report — factual and formal; article — written for publication.
The ability to read, understand, interpret and evaluate a text.
Careful, detailed reading of short texts for full understanding (study, contracts).
Reading longer texts for pleasure/ general understanding (novels, magazines).
Analysing the author's purpose, bias and evidence.
Survey (preview), Question (turn headings into questions), Read, Recite (recall in own words), Review.
Use clues — synonyms, antonyms, examples, definitions, word parts (prefix, root, suffix).
Biographies, autobiographies, memoirs, essays, travelogues, speeches, self-help.
Research papers, textbooks, abstracts — formal, technical, objective, citations.
Imagery, figurative language, rhythm.
Slogans, ads, brochures, opinion pieces.
Blogs, social media, websites, infographics.
Formal, informal, humorous, serious, optimistic, pessimistic, sarcastic, objective, critical, neutral.
(1) read the passage once for the gist; (2) read the questions; (3) re-read to find answers; (4) answer in your own words in complete sentences; (5) check grammar and word limit.
To inform, persuade, entertain, describe, instruct. Tone clues: word choice (adjectives, adverbs), figurative language.
"The company's profit rose by 12% in the third quarter, mainly due to higher exports, although costs also increased by 5%." Q: What caused the profit growth? — Higher exports.

"Renewable energy, once considered expensive, is now the cheapest source of power in many regions, and countries are rapidly expanding solar and wind farms." Main idea: renewable energy has become affordable and is expanding.
Copying whole lines; answering from outside knowledge; ignoring the question word; ignoring word limit; wrong inference; not checking the title.

How to read a report (executive summary first, then findings, conclusion, recommendations), a contract (clauses, definitions, penalty), annual report (MD&A, balance sheet, notes), email chain (latest message, action items).
The set of words a person knows and uses. Types: active (productive) — words used in speaking and writing; passive (receptive) — words understood but not used.
Clear expression, confidence in speaking, better reading comprehension, professional impression, accuracy.
Decide, decision, decisive, decisively; compounding (blackboard); conversion (a "run" / to "run").
Synonyms (similar meaning — big/ large; buy/ purchase), antonyms (opposite — expand/ contract), homophones (same sound, different spelling — their/ there;
Words that go together — make a decision, take a risk, do business, meet a deadline, heavy rain, strong tea, launch a product, close a deal, draw a conclusion.
Affect/effect, adapt/adopt, beside/besides, continual/ continuous, eminent/ imminent, farther/ further, historic/ historical, lie/ lay, precede/ proceed.
A conversation between two or more people written down. Purpose: to show how people speak and interact; used in plays, stories, language practice, business role plays.
Speaker's name followed by a colon, then the speech; each speaker begins a new line; stage directions in brackets; conversational, natural language; short sentences.

Greeting (Good morning, nice to meet you), asking (Could you tell me..., May I know...), agreeing (Absolutely, I agree), disagreeing politely (I see your point, but...), suggesting (How about..., Why don't we...), apologising (I'm sorry for the inconvenience), closing (Thank you for your time).
Formal (interview, meeting, customer service, negotiation), informal (friends, family), telephone, persuasive, problem–solution, sales (seller–buyer), complaint.
Customer: "I received a damaged phone." Support: "I am sorry to hear that. May I have your order number?" ... closing with a replacement.
The art of narrating events with characters, setting and plot to engage and communicate a message — oral, written or visual.
Beginning (exposition) → rising action → climax → falling action → resolution (denouement) (Freytag's pyramid); three-act structure; hero's journey (Joseph Campbell).
Start with a hook; use vivid sensory language ("show, don't tell"); dialogue; suspense; emotion; pace; humour; repetition; metaphors/ similes; a clear message; an ending that resonates.
Voice modulation (pitch, volume, pace), pauses, facial expressions and gestures, eye contact, posture, movement, use of props, audience interaction, practising and timing.

Know your audience; keep it simple and short; have one message; make characters relatable; use concrete details; end with a lesson; practise aloud; rehearse timing; vary tone; handle nervousness by deep breathing.
Fluency, accuracy, clarity, confidence; avoid fillers (um, you know); use the rule of three; active listening; body language; audience awareness; structure (opening–body–closing).

The accepted code of polite, respectful and professional behaviour in a social or professional setting. Business etiquette: the unwritten rules of behaviour that help people interact professionally, build trust and create a positive image.

flashcards.front: Meaning, Importance and Principles of Business Etiquette — Importance
flashcards.back: Creates a positive first impression; builds trust and relationships; improves teamwork and communication; reflects the organisation's culture and brand; avoids misunderstandings and conflict; helps in career growth; supports cross-cultural business; boosts confidence.
Respect, courtesy, punctuality, honesty and integrity, professionalism, discretion/ confidentiality, consideration, accountability, good listening, cultural sensitivity, appropriate communication.
Manners — general social politeness; etiquette — situational rules; protocol — formal rules (diplomatic, ceremonial).
Formed in the first 7–30 seconds from appearance, body language, handshake, greeting, tone.

Posture, eye contact, gestures, facial expressions, personal space (proxemics — social distance about 1.2–3.5 m), tone of voice. Avoid: crossed arms, fidgeting, pointing, slouching, looking at the phone.
Clear, specific and short ("Meeting rescheduled to 3 pm, Friday"); never blank.
"Dear Mr. Rao," (formal), "Hello Anita," (semi-formal); closing: "Yours sincerely"/ "Best regards"/ "Kind regards" + name, designation, contact.
To — main recipients; Cc — for information; Bcc — hidden copy (privacy for large groups). Reply all only when necessary. Forward carefully.
Avoid ALL CAPS (shouting), excessive exclamation marks, emojis (in formal), slang, sarcasm; do not write when angry; be respectful in complaints.
Mention them in the body; use clear file names; compress large files; check before sending.
Use calls for urgent/ sensitive matters.
Plan the purpose; call at a suitable time; identify yourself and the reason; ask "Is this a good time?"; keep it short; take notes.
Ask permission ("May I put you on hold for a moment?"); thank for waiting; do not keep callers holding long; transfer correctly — tell the caller where you are transferring.
Record caller's name, company, number, time/ date, message, action needed; repeat to confirm.
Stay calm, listen, apologise where appropriate, avoid arguing, offer solutions, escalate if needed.
Summarise action points; thank the caller; let the caller hang up first; never hang up abruptly.
"May I know who is calling?"; "Could you please spell that?"; "I am afraid he is not available"; "Can I take a message?"; "Thank you for calling."
Arrive on time; follow the dress code; wait for the host to seat guests/ begin; napkin on the lap (after the host); turn off the phone.
Wait to be seated; order moderately priced items; avoid messy dishes; follow the host's lead on courses; tell about dietary restrictions earlier.
Light topics; avoid politics, religion, personal matters; do business after ordering or at the end as per the host; include everyone; listen.
The host pays; if you invited, you pay; thank the host; tip appropriately; follow-up thank-you note.

Vegetarian/ non-vegetarian preferences; eating with the right hand where customary; washing hands; respect for elders — wait for them to start; cross-cultural — avoid beef/ pork assumptions; do not waste food.
Drink only if appropriate; limit consumption; no pressure.

Keep noise low (calls, music with headphones); do not enter without knocking/ "knocking" on the cubicle wall; no strong food smells; respect "do not disturb" signs; keep the desk tidy; do not touch others' belongings; avoid loud conversations/ speaker calls — use meeting rooms; avoid eavesdropping; moderate perfume;

Formal (suit/ saree/ salwar-kameez/ shirt-trousers, formal shoes), business casual, smart casual, casual Friday, uniform. Guidelines: clean, ironed, well-fitted clothes; modest; minimal jewellery and fragrance; neat grooming (hair, nails); appropriate footwear; adapt to the company/ occasion/ culture;
Agenda circulated; purpose clear; invite relevant people; be on time; prepare; book the room; send pre-reads.

Arrive early; silence phones; take notes; listen; don't interrupt; raise your hand/ speak when invited; stay on the topic and time; chair keeps order; respect all opinions; avoid side conversations and multitasking; greet and introduce; summarise decisions and assign actions.
Circulate the minutes (decisions, responsible persons, deadlines) within 24 hours; follow up on actions.

Test the technology; mute when not speaking; camera on if required; neutral background; good lighting; use the chat/ "raise hand" feature; look at the camera; avoid eating; join on time; share the screen carefully; record only with permission.
A sentence that is either true or false (not a question, command or exclamation).
Premise 1; Premise 2; Therefore, Conclusion.
Inference to the best explanation.
Affirming the consequent (If P then Q; Q; therefore P ✗) and denying the antecedent (If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q ✗).
A is sufficient for B if A guarantees B; A is necessary for B if B cannot occur without A.
Decision making, negotiations, audits, problem solving, data interpretation, ethics.
An error in reasoning that makes an argument unsound or invalid.
Check relevance, sufficiency and acceptability of premises; look for hidden assumptions; stay on the issue; use enough, representative evidence.
The art of effective, persuasive communication, in speech or writing (Aristotle's *Rhetoric*). Its goal is to persuade or inform a particular audience in a particular situation.

Appeal to the speaker's credibility, authority, trustworthiness and ethics. Ways: qualifications and experience, expertise, reputation, honesty, fairness, citing reliable sources, professional tone, shared values.

Appeal to reason, logic, facts, statistics, evidence, definitions, analogies, cause–effect reasoning. Example: "Studies show that a 10% reduction in energy use saves Rs 5 lakh a year." Weakness: can be dry and may fail to move people.
The right time/ occasion for the appeal (the fourth appeal added by later scholars); Telos: purpose.

Speaker (writer), audience, message (text), plus context, purpose and medium. Rhetorical devices: repetition, rhetorical question, metaphor, simile, alliteration, anaphora, antithesis, hyperbole, rule of three, irony, analogy, parallelism.

A toothpaste advertisement — "9 out of 10 dentists recommend" (ethos + logos); a charity advertisement with a crying child (pathos); a car advertisement with safety ratings (logos), a celebrity (ethos), a happy family (pathos).
Logos of brands, experts, certifications, testimonials, celebrity, the credibility of the organisation.
Emotional images, faces, children, animals, music, colours, slogans arousing feelings.
Facts, numbers, graphs, product features, comparisons, logical claims.

flashcards.front: Picture Description and Analysis of Ethos, Pathos and Logos — Evaluate effectiveness
flashcards.back: Is the balance appropriate? Is it manipulative? Who is the target? What is missing?

flashcards.front: Picture Description and Analysis of Ethos, Pathos and Logos — Write the paragraph/ essay
flashcards.back: Introduction (what the picture is and its purpose), description, analysis of ethos, pathos, logos, conclusion (overall effectiveness).
Emotional force is strong, but the poster could add data on outcomes to strengthen logos.

A structured, rule-governed discussion in which two sides present opposing arguments on a motion (resolution) to persuade an audience/ judges. Not a quarrel — focuses on reasoned argument, evidence, rebuttal and respectful exchange.
Proposition (Government/ Affirmative/ For) — supports the motion and must define it; Opposition (Negative/ Against) — rejects it. Burden of proof lies on the proposition.
Two teams of three; reply speeches; 7 minutes.
An audience votes before and after the debate.
One-on-one, value-focused; Public Forum; Policy debate (team, evidence-heavy); Karl Popper (cross-examination); World Schools style; Cross-examination debate.
Introduction (greeting, define/ signpost), Body (arguments: claim–reason–evidence–impact), Rebuttal, Conclusion (summarise, closing line).
Claim (the position), Grounds/ Data (evidence), Warrant (link between data and claim), Backing, Qualifier, Rebuttal.
Define the motion; set the framework/ model; 2–3 substantive arguments; anticipate opposition; prepare rebuttals; signpost.
Record the arguments and responses in columns to track.
Clear voice, moderate pace, eye contact, gestures, confidence, time management.
Matter (content, logic, evidence), Manner (delivery, style), Method (structure, role fulfilment), Rebuttal/ Engagement.
Research both sides; understand terms; pick strong arguments rather than many; practise; keep to time; listen carefully.
A neutral facilitator who manages the process — does not take sides.

flashcards.front: How to Moderate a Debate — Before
flashcards.back: Understand the motion and format; prepare the rules and time limits; coordinate with timekeepers and judges; set up the room and the speaking order; brief the speakers.

flashcards.front: How to Moderate a Debate — Opening
flashcards.back: Welcome the audience; introduce the motion, the teams, the judges and the rules; explain timing signals and POI rules.
Invite questions; ensure fairness; avoid long statements; paraphrase unclear questions.

flashcards.front: How to Moderate a Debate — Closing
flashcards.back: Thank participants; summarise (neutrally); announce adjudication/ voting procedures; declare results (if required) and close with courtesy.
Neutrality, fairness, authority with politeness, knowledge of the format, time sense, active listening, clear voice, tact, quick thinking, respectful, composed under pressure.

Ethical — strong evidence, logical rebuttal, clear structure; unethical — personal attacks, distortion, shouting down, "gish gallop" (overwhelming with many weak points), misrepresenting opponents, hidden agenda.
Debate promotes free speech, accountability and informed decisions.

flashcards.front: Both-Side-Ism, Fallacy of Relativism and Principle of Cha... — Note
flashcards.back: Debate training requires arguing either side, which is a skill exercise and not a claim that both sides are equal; the judge's role is to assess the quality of argument.
The mistaken belief that "all views/ truths are equally valid" or "truth is relative to each person", therefore no view can be judged right or wrong.

flashcards.front: Both-Side-Ism, Fallacy of Relativism and Principle of Cha... — Benefits
flashcards.back: Reduces misunderstanding; builds trust and civility; improves the quality of debate; makes rebuttals stronger and fairer; promotes learning; helps negotiation and conflict resolution.
Charity doesn't mean accepting bad arguments, pretending a fallacy isn't one, or ignoring clear intent; apply reasonable charity.
Straw man — distort to defeat easily; charity — strengthen to engage honestly.
"This House believes that remote work should be the default for office jobs."):
A structured oral (and visual) communication of information, ideas or findings to an audience to inform, persuade or demonstrate.
Rule — about 1–2 minutes per slide; opening 10%, body 80%, closing 10%.
Presents a project's problem, objectives, method, findings and recommendations — e.g. a market research project, feasibility study, business plan, case study, internship report, product launch.

flashcards.front: Structure and Content of the Presentation — Opening
flashcards.back: Greeting, hook (question, story, fact, quote, statistic), introduce yourself/ team, topic and objective, agenda/ roadmap.

flashcards.front: Structure and Content of the Presentation — Body
flashcards.back: 3–5 key points, each with evidence, examples and visuals; transitions ("Moving on to...", "As we can see...").

flashcards.front: Structure and Content of the Presentation — Closing
flashcards.back: Summary of key points; conclusion/ recommendations; call to action; thank you and invitation for questions.
Problem → solution → benefits; use stories and analogies; connect with the audience.

"Analysing UPI Adoption among College Students" — Problem: limited understanding of digital payment behaviour; Objective: study the extent and reasons for UPI usage; Method: a survey of 100 students; Findings: 92% use UPI daily; top reasons — convenience and cashback; main concern — fraud;
Clutter, too many colours, heavy animation, low-quality images, copyright violations, spelling errors.
10 slides, 20 minutes, 30-point minimum font (for pitch).
Alignment, white space, rule of thirds, visual hierarchy.
Blue — trust; green — growth; red — urgency; avoid red-green combos (colour-blind).
Whiteboard, handouts, flip charts, models, props, demonstrations, posters.
Alt-text, large font, captions, colour-blind-friendly palette.

flashcards.front: Delivery, Group Presentations and Q&A — Verbal
flashcards.back: Clear voice, moderate pace, volume, pauses, emphasis, avoid fillers, simple language, vary tone.
Questions, polls, stories, examples, humour (appropriate), interaction, demos.
Backup (USB, cloud), PDF copy, adapters, a plan B without slides.
Coordinator/ leader, researcher, designer, speaker(s), timekeeper, Q&A responders.
Unequal speaking time; reading from the slides; arguing in front of the audience; unprepared handovers.
Seek and use feedback; self-evaluation; peer review; reflection.
